params.question: All the major DNA viruses that cause cutaneous infections establish latency in sensory nerve ganglia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect — the statement is false. Ganglion latency is specific to the Herpesviridae (HSV and VZV). Papillomaviruses infect keratinocytes and the molluscum poxvirus replicates in the epidermis — neither establishes neural latency. This distinction is why recurrence patterns and treatment strategies differ by virus family.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Only the Herpesviridae (HSV and VZV) establish latency in sensory ganglia, which explains their characteristic pattern of recurrence. Papillomaviruses infect keratinocytes without neural latency, and the poxvirus causing molluscum replicates in the epidermis.

interactions.label: Which feature of the varicella rash most reliably distinguishes it from smallpox

params.question: Which feature of the varicella rash most reliably distinguishes it from smallpox?

answers.text: All lesions progressing through the same developmental stage simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Monomorphism — all lesions at the same stage — is characteristic of smallpox, not varicella. Varicella shows the opposite pattern.

answers.text: A rash that is denser on the extremities than on the trunk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A centrifugal distribution (denser on extremities) is a feature of smallpox. Varicella has a centripetal distribution, meaning it is denser on the trunk and face.

answers.text: Lesions present in multiple stages of evolution at the same time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Varicella shows polymorphism — macules, papules, vesicles and crusts are visible simultaneously because new crops keep appearing over several days. In smallpox all lesions are at the same stage.

answers.text: Absence of a febrile prodrome before the rash appears

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Varicella typically begins with fever and malaise before the eruption. A febrile prodrome occurs in both varicella and smallpox and does not help distinguish them.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: the key distinction is polymorphism. In varicella, new crops of lesions keep appearing, so macules, vesicles and crusts coexist at any given moment — unlike smallpox, where all lesions evolve in synchrony.
Well done. Polymorphism — the simultaneous presence of lesions at different stages — is the hallmark that separates varicella from smallpox at the bedside.

interactions.label: What is the defining recognition feature that allows a confident bedside diagnos

params.question: What is the defining recognition feature that allows a confident bedside diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum?

answers.text: A rough, hyperkeratotic surface with thrombosed capillary dots

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Interrupted dermatoglyphics and thrombosed capillary ('black dot') puncta are the morphological signature of viral warts caused by HPV, not molluscum contagiosum.

answers.text: A central umbilication in a pearly, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papule

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The central dimple (umbilication) in a firm, smooth, pearly papule is pathognomonic for molluscum contagiosum. Once you train your eye for this feature, the diagnosis can be made at a glance.

answers.text: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with a tingling prodrome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base preceded by a tingling prodrome describe herpes simplex (HSV), not molluscum contagiosum.

answers.text: A polymorphic rash with macules, vesicles and crusts present simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A polymorphic eruption with lesions at different stages coexisting is the hallmark of varicella (chickenpox), not molluscum contagiosum.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: molluscum contagiosum presents as firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with a characteristic central dimple (umbilication) — distinct from the vesicles of herpes, the verrucous surface of warts, or the polymorphic rash of varicella.
Excellent. The central umbilication is the single most important clue — look for it in every dome-shaped papule you encounter.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old man presents with multiple common warts on his hands. Which manage

params.question: A 30-year-old man presents with multiple common warts on his hands. Which management approach is most appropriate?

answers.text: Start oral aciclovir to prevent further spread

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Aciclovir acts on herpesvirus DNA polymerase and has no activity against human papillomavirus. No systemic antiviral exists for HPV infections.
Incorrect. Valaciclovir is the prodrug of aciclovir, effective against herpesviruses only. It has no role in managing HPV-induced warts.

answers.text: Offer physical destruction (e.g. cryotherapy) or watchful waiting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. No systemic antiviral exists for HPV. Warts are managed by physical destruction (cryotherapy, electrocautery, salicylic acid) or by watchful waiting, since many resolve spontaneously as host immunity develops.

answers.text: Isolate the patient and initiate contact tracing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While counselling about transmission is appropriate, common warts are not a notifiable disease and do not require isolation or contact tracing.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: unlike herpesviruses, HPV has no systemic antiviral. Warts are managed by physical destruction (cryotherapy, salicylic acid) or watchful waiting, since many resolve as the host's immune response develops.
Well done. Recognising that HPV has no systemic antiviral is the key management distinction — treatment is either destruction or patience.
